equal_ask: Go on, then. Move my coins to him until we're even.

r1_flip: Then we flip this coin. Blue side, you win. Red side, I win.
r1_odds: Fifty-fifty? I've bet on worse odds.

r2_go: Smart. Okay, let's go. I'll win it back.
rules_1: Both bet half. Flip. The color that lands takes both.
rules_2: Both bet half of what the poorer one has.
rules_3: …and two people are picked at random each time.
dare_ahead: Back where we started. Well, I'm a bit ahead. Naturally.
dare_edge: Nobody has an edge. Same odds, same rules. Nobody gets rich.
dare_what: But what if one of us did? Very rich.
dare_imagine: Imagine it happens anyway. What would that tell you?
dare_luck: That being rich means nothing. No talent, no hard work. Just luck.
dare_bet: I'll bet half my wealth you can't.
dare_sure: All of it? You're either very sure or very foolish.
more_add: Two players can't settle this. Let's add more people.
more_hundred: A hundred. Everyone starts equal. Including us.
more_random: Each time, two people are picked at random. Same bet. Same coin.
more_real: Real life is much more complicated than this, you know.
more_joke: Of course it is. Want to hear a joke first?

gini_1: Economists love a single number. What's ours?
gini_2: Watch it being built. Zero means everyone has the same.
gini_3: One is the far edge: one owner, everyone else at nothing.
eff_1: A hundred players. That's a lot of competition.
eff_2: Is it? Start with four. Move the coins yourself.
eff_one: Four people, one player. Me, I hope.
eff_3: Four bodies still in the room. The number counts the field they have left.
participation_formula: Open the black box: write each person's share of the room as sᵢ. Square the shares, add them, then take the reciprocal: 1 / Σsᵢ². This is the inverse Herfindahl concentration index.
turn_1: The trade counter keeps racing. But most people have almost nothing left to bet.
turn_2: So a million trades can move almost nothing.
turn_3: Right. So we count the money that actually changes hands.
turn_def: One measurement round is one trade per person on average. Ordinary turnover adds the stakes that crossed between people in that round and divides by all the wealth in the room. 0.30 roomfuls means wealth equal to 30% of the room changed hands.
crowd_1: Surely a bigger crowd evens things out.
crowd_2: A thousand people. Two million fair trades. Let's see.
end_1: Fine. But a run is just one run.
end_2: True. Now the proof I promised you.
end_3: Keep going without end, and one owner takes it all. That's proven.
end_5: It is. It's a limit, not a date.
end_7: The name changes. The shape doesn't.
end_citation: For a fixed finite number of agents and a fixed stake fraction 0 < β < 1, the wealth vector converges almost surely to one of the room's one-owner states. "Almost surely" means probability one; it does not mean every imaginable sequence of coin tosses. The proof is in Börgers & Greengard (2023).
stake_1: Then make the bets smaller. Problem solved.
stake_2: Try it. Smaller bets take longer. They still get there.
stake_4: Zero isn't a slow game. It's no game.

tax_2: I want you to try. Keep at least twenty players in the game.
tax_3: Tap a big fortune. A quarter goes into a pool, shared equally by everyone.
tax_4: Tax me too much and I stop building.
tax_5: Fair point. In this world nobody builds. They only trade. So we test the math alone.
tax_after_1: Notice what your hand did. It picked one person, again and again.
tax_after_3: Then let's write it into the rules.
levy_1: Same percentage from everyone. One pool. Shared back equally.
levy_3: Watch the return. Below average gains. Average breaks even. Above pays in.
match_1: Same luck, same trades, twice. Only one room gets the rule.
match_2: So luck can't take the credit.

map_3: That line is my challenge, not a law of nature.
